newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Solana says optimistic on Russia-NATO talks.
newsitem.headline: Solana says optimistic on Russia-NATO talks.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said on his arrival in the Kazakh capital Almaty on Monday that talks between the Western alliance and Russia were "moving in the right direction".

"There are still problems but we are moving in the right direction, I think," Solana told reporters at Almaty airport, where he was met in snowy weather by an honour guard and senior Kazakh officials.
Solana had flown east after meeting Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on Sunday to kick off a five-day tour of the former Soviet republics of Central Asia.
"Positive work was done," the Russian Foreign Ministry said in a statement following the meeting with Primakov. But it added: "Differences remain on a range of problems."
Moscow and NATO are at odds over the plans for the alliance to invite in new members at a July summit in Madrid. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are favourites to be the first new entries.
Solana told reporters in Almaty he had come to discuss the participation of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan in NATO's "Partnership for Peace" programme.
The fifth former Soviet republic of Central Asia, Tajikistan, devastated by a four-year civil war and prey to a motley array of armed bands, is not on Solana's itinerary.
Solana's last swing through the ex-Soviet republics in February prompted a stream of invective from the Kremlin over plans for NATO expansion.
Russia is very sensitive to NATO involvement in the former Soviet republics, but the alliance's Moscow representative John Lough defended Solana's trip.
"These talks are transparent. There is no hidden agenda," Lough told Reuters.
"We see no fundamental incompatibility in the relation of these countries with Russia and with NATO through the Partnership for Peace," he said.
Under the programme, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan will carry out a joint 10-day peace-keeping exercise with NATO on Kazakh and Uzbek territory in September.

Western diplomats in Almaty played down NATO aims in the region and said the alliance's expansion was only an issue for the Central Asian states in terms of its effect on their former colonial overlord, Russia.
"Partnership for Peace is about as far as they're likely to go," said one diplomat. "The region is very distant from the NATO area," he said.
